title: Learning data.table Notes
text:
Preface
My notes on learning data.table.

title: Learning data.table Notes
text:
Basics

data.table()


library(data.table)
small_dtb <- data.table(x = letters[1:5],
                        y = rnorm(5),
                        z = 1:5)
small_dtb

        x          y     z
   <char>      <num> <int>
1:      a  0.7483929     1
2:      b  0.4520126     2
3:      c  1.2175161     3
4:      d  1.4380206     4
5:      e -0.3924529     5



You can also convert existing objects to a data.table using setDT() (for data.frame and list structures) or as.data.table() (for other structures).


general form DT[i, j, by] — Take DT, subset/reorder rows using i, then calculate j, grouped by by.
subset rows in i

Example:

(small_dtb[x %in% c('a', 'b', 'c', 'e') & z >= 3])

        x          y     z
   <char>      <num> <int>
1:      c  1.2175161     3
2:      e -0.3924529     5


Example:

(small_dtb[c(2, 5)])

        x          y     z
   <char>      <num> <int>
1:      b  0.4520126     2
2:      e -0.3924529     5


up to – Sort flights first by column origin in ascending order, and then by dest in descending order:

title: 1  Introduction to data.table
text:
1.1 Basics
library(data.table)

set.seed(12345)

small_dtb <- data.table(x = letters[1:5],
                        y = rnorm(5),
                        z = 1:5)
small_dtb

        x          y     z
   <char>      <num> <int>
1:      a  0.5855288     1
2:      b  0.7094660     2
3:      c -0.1093033     3
4:      d -0.4534972     4
5:      e  0.6058875     5
Example:
(small_dtb[x %in% c('a', 'b', 'c', 'e') & z >= 3])

        x          y     z
   <char>      <num> <int>
1:      c -0.1093033     3
2:      e  0.6058875     5
Example:
(small_dtb[c(2, 5)])

        x         y     z
   <char>     <num> <int>
1:      b 0.7094660     2
2:      e 0.6058875     5
Example:
# x in in descending order; and then y in ascending order
(small_dtb[order(-x, y)])

        x          y     z
   <char>      <num> <int>
1:      e  0.6058875     5
2:      d -0.4534972     4
3:      c -0.1093033     3
4:      b  0.7094660     2
5:      a  0.5855288     1
Example:
(small_dtb[, .(x, z)])

        x     z
   <char> <int>
1:      a     1
2:      b     2
3:      c     3
4:      d     4
5:      e     5
Example:
# select and rename
(small_dtb[, .(x_1 = x, z)])

      x_1     z

1:      a     1
2:      b     2
3:      c     3
4:      d     4
5:      e     5
Example:
# return a vector
(small_dtb[, z])

[1] 1 2 3 4 5

(small_dtb)

        x          y     z

(chk <- small_dtb[, sum(y + z > 3)])

(small_dtb[x %in% letters[2:4], sum(y + z > 3)])

[1] 1

       mean_1 mean_2
        <num>  <num>
1: 0.04888851      3
Example:
(small_dtb[x %in% c('a', 'c', 'f') & y > 0, .N])

[1] 1

title: 1  Introduction to data.table
text:
data.table()



You can also convert existing objects to a data.table using setDT() (for data.frame and list structures) or as.data.table() (for other structures).


General form DT[i, j, by] — Take DT, subset/reorder rows using i, then calculate j, grouped by by.
Subset rows in i






Order rows




Select column(s) in j




Tip: As long as j-expression returns a list, each element of the list will be converted to a column in the resulting data.table.






Compute or do in j




Subset in i and do in j






Special symbol .N


.N is a special built-in variable that holds the number of observations in the current group.




Select columns named in a variable using with = FALSE




with = FALSE tells data.table to treat sel_vars as column names (a character vector), not as an expression to evaluate.


Deselect columns using - or !






Select by specifying start and end column names (From version 1.9.5+)

          y = sample(month.abb, length(ID), replace = TRUE),
          w = runif(length(ID)),

title: 2  Reference semantics
text:
2.1 Syntax
The LHS := RHS form
DT[, c("colA", "colB", ...) := list(valA, valB, ...)]
# when you have only one column to assign to you
# can drop the quotes and list(), for convenience
DT[, colA := valA]
The functional form
DT[, `:=`(colA = valA, # valA is assigned to colA
          colB = valB, # valB is assigned to colB
         )
  ]

title: 2  Reference semantics
text:
In “LHS := RHS form”, LHS takes a character vector of column names and RHS a list of values. RHS just needs to be a list, irrespective of how its generated (e.g., using lapply(), list(), mget(), mapply() etc.). This form is usually easy to program with and is particularly useful when you don’t know the columns to assign values to in advance.




In the two forms of := shown above, note that we don’t assign the result back to a variable. Because we don’t need to. The input data.table is modified by reference.

title: 2  Reference semantics
text:
2.3 :=andcopy()`

:= modifies the input object by reference. Apart from the features we have discussed already, sometimes we might want to use the update by reference feature for its side effect. And at other times it may not be desirable to modify the original object, in which case we can use copy() function, as we will see in a moment.

Example:

(dt_1)

        ID      u         v           x         x_1        w_1 count new_grp
    <char> <char>    <char>       <num>       <num>      <num> <int>  <char>
 1:     01      a   January  1.61095311  1.52246017 0.36640648     2       A
 2:     02      b  February  0.28500060  0.08452287 0.03026150     2       A
 3:     03      c     March  1.71420451  1.63443178 1.73189933     2       A
 4:     04      d     April -0.66211776 -0.94258541 0.31665220     1       A
 5:     05      e       May  0.64469837  0.47459932 1.60921663     1       A
 6:     06      f      June -0.87407021 -1.17243853 1.74539633     1       B
 7:     07      g      July -0.27447155 -0.52220011 1.71124976     1       B
 8:     08      h    August -0.07836709 -0.30953343 1.78824395     1       B
 9:     09      i September  0.59936720  0.42543966 0.39686535     1       B
10:     10      j   October  0.96864272  0.82590275 0.46928588     1       B
11:     11      k  November -1.31463863 -1.65021564 1.89316502     1       C
12:     12      l  December  0.77092541  0.61148700 0.22828796     1       C
13:     13      m   January  0.75896271  0.59851397 1.52812948     2       C
14:     14      n  February -0.02522628 -0.25190455 0.45504884     2       C
15:     15      o     March -1.01795922 -1.32847985 0.09553725     2       C

my_fun_1 <- function(a_dt)
{a_dt[, the_sum := x_1 + w_1][
      , .(the_max = max(the_sum)), by = new_grp]
}

(my_fun_1(dt_1))

   new_grp  the_max
    <char>    <num>
1:       A 3.366331
2:       B 1.478711
3:       C 2.126643

(names(dt_1))

[1] "ID"      "u"       "v"       "x"       "x_1"     "w_1"     "count"  
[8] "new_grp" "the_sum"

# remove `the_sum` from dt_1
dt_1[, the_sum := NULL]
(names(dt_1))

[1] "ID"      "u"       "v"       "x"       "x_1"     "w_1"     "count"  
[8] "new_grp"

# use copy()
my_fun_2 <- function(a_dt)
{a_dt <- copy(a_dt)
 a_dt[, the_sum := x_1 + w_1][
      , .(the_max = max(the_sum)), by = new_grp]
}

(my_fun_2(dt_1))

   new_grp  the_max
    <char>    <num>
1:       A 3.366331
2:       B 1.478711
3:       C 2.126643

(names(dt_1))

[1] "ID"      "u"       "v"       "x"       "x_1"     "w_1"     "count"  
[8] "new_grp"



When we store the column names on to a variable, e.g., DT_n = names(DT), and then add/update/delete column(s) by reference. It would also modify DT_n, unless we do copy(names(DT)).


DT <- data.table(x = 1L, y = 2L)
(DT_n  <-  names(DT))

[1] "x" "y"

## add a new column by reference
DT[, z := 3L][]

       x     y     z
   <int> <int> <int>
1:     1     2     3

## DT_n also gets updated
(DT_n)

[1] "x" "y" "z"

## use `copy()`
DT_n = copy(names(DT))
DT[, w := 4L]

## DT_n doesn't get updated
(DT_n)

[1] "x" "y" "z"



When you extract a single column as a vector, there is a subtle but important difference between standard R methods ($ and [[…]]) and data.table’s j expression. DT$col and DT[[‘col’]] may return a reference to the column, while DT[, col] always returns a copy.

To select a single column as a vector, remember:

DT[, mycol] is safer as it always returns a new, independent copy.
DT$mycol is fast but may return a reference. Use copy(DT$mycol) to guarantee independence.

title: 2  Reference semantics
text:
2.4 Summary
The := operator

It is used to add/update/delete columns by reference.
We can use := for its side effect or use copy() to not modify the original object while updating by reference.

When you extract a single column as a vector, there is a subtle but important difference between standard R methods ($ and [[…]]) and data.table’s j expression. DT$col and DT[[‘col’]] may return a reference to the column, while DT[, col] always returns a copy.

To select a single column as a vector, remember:

DT[, mycol] is safer as it always returns a new, independent copy.
DT$mycol is fast but may return a reference. Use copy(DT$mycol) to guarantee independence.

title: 3  Keys and fast binary search based subset
text:
3.1 Keys
Keys and their properties
crumbs: 3  Keys and fast binary search based subset

title: 3  Keys and fast binary search based subset
text:
data.tables never uses row names. Since data.tables inherit from data.frames, it still has the row names attribute. But it never uses them.


If you would like to preserve the row names, use keep.rownames = TRUE in as.data.table(a_df) - this will create a new column called rn and assign row names to this column.


Instead, in data.tables we set and use keys. Think of a key as supercharged rownames.



We can set keys on multiple columns.
Uniqueness is not enforced, i.e., duplicate key values are allowed. Since rows are sorted by key, any duplicates in the key columns will appear consecutively.
Setting a key does two things

physically reorders the rows of the data.table by the column(s) provided by reference, always in increasing order. (Since the rows are reordered, a data.table can have at most one key because it can not be sorted in more than one way.)
marks those columns as key columns by setting an attribute called sorted to the data.table.

8.8 data.table programming
Notice using get function and setNames(list(.N), output_var_name) in the following code.

library(data.table)

my_aggregate <- function(a_dt, condi_var_nm = NULL, 
                         condi = c('1', '2'), output_var_name = NULL)
{if(is.null(condi_var_nm)) {
  return(a_dt[, .(total = .N), by = partition_code][order(partition_code)]) }
  a_dt[get(condi_var_nm) %in% condi, setNames(list(.N), output_var_name), 
       by = partition_code][order(partition_code)]   
}

set.seed(123)
fk_dt <- data.table(id = 1:60,
                    maori = sample(c('0', '1', '2'), 60, replace = TRUE),
                    asian = sample(c('0', '1', '2'), 60, replace = TRUE),
                    pacific = sample(c('0', '1', '2'), 60, replace = TRUE),
                    rand_nbr = runif(60))
fk_dt[order(rand_nbr), partition_code := (.I - 1) %% 3 + 1]

total_dt <- my_aggregate(fk_dt)
maori_dt <- my_aggregate(fk_dt, condi_var_nm = "maori", output_var_name = "maori")
asian <- my_aggregate(fk_dt, condi_var_nm = "asian", 
                      condi = '1', output_var_name = "asian")
pacific <- my_aggregate(fk_dt, condi_var_nm = "pacific", output_var_name = "pacific")

j <- 
  merge(total_dt, maori_dt, by = 'partition_code', all.x = TRUE) |>
  merge(asian, by = 'partition_code', all.x = TRUE) |>
  merge(pacific, by = 'partition_code', all.x = TRUE)

title: 4  Secondary indices and auto indexing
text:
Secondary indices are similar to keys in data.table, except for two major differences:



It doesn’t physically reorder the entire data.table in RAM. Instead, it only computes the order for the set of columns provided and stores that order vector in an additional attribute called index.




There can be more than one secondary index for a data.table (as we will see below).

title: 4  Secondary indices and auto indexing
text:
4.2 How

setindex() and setindexv() allows adding a secondary index to the data.table.
The function indices() returns all current secondary indices in the data.table. If none exists, NULL is returned.
setindex(dt, NULL) would remove all secondary indices
on argument

enables subsetting by computing secondary indices on the fly. This eliminates having to do setindex() every time.
allows easy reuse of existing indices by just checking the attributes.
allows for a cleaner syntax by having the columns on which the subset is performed as part of the syntax. This makes the code easier to follow when looking at it at a later point.

title: 6  Fast Read and Fast Write
text:
fread() can read data directly from web URLs by passing the URL as a character string to its file argument.




fread automates delimiter and header detection, eliminating the need for manual specification in most cases. You simply provide the filename—fread intelligently detects the structure



Many real-world datasets contain columns that are initially blank, zero-filled, or appear numeric but later contain characters. To handle such inconsistencies, fread() employs a robust column type detection strategy.



To save memory and improve performance, use fread()’s select or drop arguments to read only the columns you need.
